clips.text_zh: >Oil >Uranium >Copper >Gold >Silver 全部都係未來15年嘅play。Tech根本唔使睇。Prop firm個倉又輸緊，又係學費😭🙏
clips.text_en_b1: The /biz/ thesis for the next 15 years is oil, uranium, copper, gold, and silver. The OP says you will outperform tech with this list. No charts, no entry levels — just a strong opinion that commodities beat tech. Hard assets over paper promises, basically.
clips.text_en_b2: The /biz/ thesis lays out a fifteen-year conviction play built around oil, uranium, copper, gold, and silver, dismissing tech entirely as overpriced noise. The poster argues these commodities will outperform equities simply because hard assets outlast paper promises. No charts, no entry levels, and no technical analysis appear anywhere in the thread, just an aggressive stance that bets against the entire tech sector. Meanwhile, the same poster admits his prop firm account is bleeding again, calling it another painful lesson paid for out of pocket.
clips.text_en_c1: The prevailing thesis circulating on /biz/ holds that the coming fifteen years will be defined by a commodities supercycle, with oil, uranium, copper, gold, and silver positioned to outperform virtually every other asset class. The original poster dismisses the technology sector entirely, arguing that anyone still allocating capital to tech equities has fundamentally misread the macroeconomic landscape. Notably, no charts, entry points, or supporting data accompany the claim. The underlying conviction is straightforward: hard, tangible assets, whose value derives from physical scarcity rather than corporate earnings projections, will inevitably eclipse paper-based instruments and speculative growth narratives over the long term.
clips.text_en_c2: The /biz/ thesis for the coming fifteen years is, in essence, a wholesale pivot away from technology and toward tangible commodities — oil, uranium, copper, gold, and silver, presented not as a diversified basket but as the singular macro trade. The poster argues, with a conviction bordering on evangelism, that hard assets will systematically outperform any tech-equity proxy over the long horizon. No charts, no entry levels, no defined risk parameters — merely the assertion that commodities represent real value while paper promises, by contrast, constitute little more than deferred disappointment. The accompanying tone is unapologetically didactic, as though the author has transcended the noise of the cycle itself. Whether the thesis merits consideration or constitutes mere contrarian posturing remains, of course, an entirely separate matter for which the reader must adjudicate.

clips.text_zh: 成班e-celeb日日話NVIDIA貴，點解唔買AMD？ROCm都work，pytorch都support。唔係啦大佬，我連GPU都冇，trade緊CFD輸緊錢先真😭👍
clips.text_en_b1: The OP asks why everyone complains about Nvidia prices instead of just buying AMD. ROCm works with PyTorch, ray tracing barely matters, and Nvidia does not even run well on Linux. AMD got a smaller price bump this generation. Buying AMD is the obvious move, he says.
clips.text_en_b2: The OP challenges anyone whining about Nvidia's inflated pricing to seriously look at AMD instead, pointing out that ROCm already runs PyTorch workloads and that ray tracing barely matters for actual compute tasks. Nvidia, he argues, barely works properly on Linux anyway, and AMD saw a smaller price hike this generation, making it the more obvious buy. The thread's punchline, however, comes when the poster admits he cannot even afford a real GPU and is currently bleeding money trading CFDs on the side, which undercuts…
clips.text_en_c1: The original poster poses a deceptively simple question: if Nvidia's valuation has become untenable, why is the broader investment community not redirecting capital toward AMD? His argument rests on several technical observations. ROCm, AMD's open-source compute platform, now integrates with PyTorch workflows, while ray tracing performance, often cited as Nvidia's decisive advantage, carries minimal weight for machine learning applications. Furthermore, Nvidia's driver stack remains notoriously unstable on Linux distributions. Given that AMD's price appreciation this generation has been considerably more measured, the logical inference, he contends, is that AMD represents the asymmetric trade that rational allocators should be pursuing instead.
clips.text_en_c2: The OP, weary of the daily chorus decrying Nvidia's stratospheric valuation, poses what he considers a self-evident rebuttal: why not simply acquire AMD? ROCm, he notes with some exasperation, already functions compatibly with PyTorch; ray-tracing superiority is, in his estimation, marginal at best; and Nvidia's driver stack, notoriously recalcitrant on Linux, scarcely justifies the premium. AMD, having received a comparatively modest price uplift this generation, ostensibly represents the rational asymmetric bet. Whether such logic constitutes genuine analytical insight or merely the familiar contrarian reflex of an online crowd remains debatable — yet the conviction with which it is delivered suggests the poster considers the matter conclusively settled.

clips.text_zh: 今日睇返slope investigation啲筆記。Factor of safety要check soil nailing spacing同groundwater table。Tommy問我GI report邊part未填，我講唔出😭 FE考牌都未溫完。
clips.text_en_b1: A /biz/ anon shared his trading losses. He estimates $50k to $75k from bad decisions over the years. The list includes fake gold chains, gambling, stocks, options, crypto, loans to other people, lawyers, drinking, and drugs. OP is asking how much other anons wasted on their own dumb mistakes.
clips.text_en_b2: A civil engineering student is cramming slope survey notes ahead of his FE exam and still cannot remember which sections of the GI report Tommy asked him to fill in yesterday. The key checks involve verifying soil nailing spacing against the factor of safety, while also accounting for fluctuations in the groundwater table during rainy season. He admits the licensing exam is far from fully revised, so he is basically winging it through site meetings while praying nothing too technical comes up.
clips.text_en_c1: Reviewing slope investigation notes reveals the critical interplay between soil nailing spacing, the prevailing groundwater table, and the resultant factor of safety calculations that govern slope stability assessments. A colleague named Tommy has inquired which section of the geotechnical interpretation report remains incomplete, and the honest answer is that the author cannot recall. With the Fundamentals of Engineering examination looming and preparation far from adequate, the situation has devolved into a familiar pattern of academic triage. If the report cannot be finished coherently before the deadline, the professional embarrassment will likely prove more damaging than any licensing setback.
clips.text_en_c2: Today's revision session returned me to the fundamentals of slope investigation, a discipline in which the factor of safety cannot be meaningfully evaluated without concurrent consideration of soil-nailing spacing and the prevailing groundwater table — two variables whose interplay, if neglected, renders any subsequent calculation fundamentally compromised. Tommy, in his characteristic fashion, inquired which section of the GI report remained incomplete; I found myself, rather embarrassingly, unable to articulate the answer with any precision. The FE professional examination, looming with its customary inevitability, has yet to receive adequate preparation, and the gap between aspirational competence and current fluency grows, if anything, more conspicuous with each passing evening.

clips.text_zh: 今日覆習beam同column個load path。RC design要check moment同shear transfer。Sum Ho何生聽日site meeting，我驚自己講唔清個detail。考牌救命🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Another /biz/ anon bragged that his mentality changed after hitting six figures. He traded crypto since late 2017 and lost everything several times. Now he has $300k, 80% in stables earning 5% APY, 1 BTC, and he is diversifying into silver and gold.
clips.text_en_b2: An engineering student is reviewing beam-to-column load path behaviour for tomorrow's site meeting with Sum Ho, and he is genuinely terrified of fumbling the technical detail in front of the senior. The revision covers reinforced concrete design principles, particularly how moment and shear transfer through joints has to be checked before any member sizing gets finalised. He admits the professional licensing exam is nowhere near ready, so he is essentially relying on muscle memory and sheer luck to survive the morning.
clips.text_en_c1: Revisiting reinforced concrete design principles requires careful attention to the load path through beams and columns, with particular emphasis on moment and shear transfer mechanisms at the connections. Tomorrow's site meeting with Mr. Sum Ho demands articulate articulation of these structural nuances, yet the underlying anxiety stems from insufficient familiarity with the granular details. Should the panel probe beyond surface-level explanations, the consequences could derail both the project's progression and the author's professional credibility. The Fundamentals of Engineering examination, still inadequately prepared for, compounds the pressure.
clips.text_en_c2: Today's review of beam-and-column load paths reaffirmed what ought to be axiomatic yet somehow eludes consistent application: in RC design, one must rigorously verify both moment and shear transfer mechanisms, for a structure is only as sound as the continuity of its load path. Sum Ho's site meeting tomorrow carries the customary apprehension, given that articulating technical detail under scrutiny requires a fluency I cannot yet guarantee. The professional examination, meanwhile, looms with its characteristic disregard for one's preparedness, and revision proceeds at a pace that suggests insufficient alarm. The broader irony — that civil engineers routinely exhort others to verify their foundations whilst neglecting their own — is not lost on me, though such recognition offers, admittedly, scant consolation when one cannot confidently trace a load through a simple portal frame.

clips.text_zh: tim apple又搞嘢。個OS偷睇你每個cursor同keystroke，仲用AI 24/7 scan你個screen。AI真係連desktop都入侵緊lol。靠AI續命都要小心🧐
clips.text_en_b1: /g/ is asking what Tim Apple meant when he said the new OS spies on every cursor movement and keystroke. It also uses AI to scan every frame of your screen 24 hours a day. The OP wants to know if this is real privacy news or just another Apple announcement.
clips.text_en_b2: /g/ is picking apart Tim Cook's claim that the new OS monitors every cursor movement and keystroke while running AI-driven screen analysis around the clock. The poster wants to know whether this constitutes genuine privacy-breaking news or merely another staged Apple announcement dressed up in marketing language. The thread assumes the worst, treating the feature as outright surveillance rather than a productivity tool, and jokes that AI has officially invaded even the average user's desktop environment at this point.
clips.text_en_c1: /g/ is dissecting Tim Cook's recent remarks regarding Apple's operating system, which allegedly monitors every cursor movement and keystroke in real time. Beyond mere keystroke logging, the system purportedly deploys artificial intelligence to scan the user's screen continuously, analyzing each frame around the clock. If these claims hold any credibility, they represent a paradigm shift in surveillance architecture. The original poster remains skeptical, however, questioning whether this constitutes genuine privacy violation warranting regulatory scrutiny, or merely another theatrical Apple keynote designed to manufacture concern. The distinction between substantive privacy erosion and marketing spectacle has never been more consequential for end users.
clips.text_en_c2: /g/ is presently dissecting Tim Cook's recent remarks — 'Tim Apple,' as the faithful insist on rendering him — concerning the new operating system's purportedly omniscient surveillance architecture. According to the OP, the OS now captures every cursor movement and keystroke with industrial thoroughness, whilst an embedded AI layer continuously scans each frame of the user's screen on a twenty-four-hour basis. The question, posed with characteristic /g/ scepticism, is whether this constitutes genuine privacy newsworthy of sustained outrage or merely the latest iteration of Apple's familiar announcement cadence dressed in theatrical garments. The broader context — that AI has, with quiet inevitability, colonised even the desktop environment — lends the inquiry a weightier philosophical dimension than its breezy tone might initially suggest, particularly for those who had hoped the personal computer might constitute a final…
clips.source_hint: /g/ panicking about Apple OS AI spying

clips.text_zh: China公開送super武器去Iran。西方根本睇唔明呢啲tech。國際版圖又變緊，個prop firm又喺度輸⋯⋯真係睇完新聞再睇個倉wtf。
clips.text_en_b1: /pol/ says China has started openly delivering superweapons to Iran. The post claims the technologies are beyond Western comprehension and are arriving in large numbers. No proof, no sources, just a short claim that the balance of power in the Middle East is shifting fast.
clips.text_en_b2: /pol/ claims China has begun openly shipping superweapons to Iran, insisting that the underlying technologies involved are beyond anything Western defence analysts can properly comprehend. The post alleges large quantities of this hardware are arriving on schedule, with no sourced evidence or verifiable sourcing to back the claim up. Despite the dramatic geopolitical framing about the Middle Eastern balance of power shifting fast, the poster signs off by checking his prop firm account and discovering yet another losing position waiting for him.
clips.text_en_c1: A /pol/ thread claims that China has commenced openly delivering sophisticated weaponry systems to Iran, with technologies so advanced that Western intelligence communities allegedly cannot even comprehend their operational parameters. The post asserts these transfers are occurring at scale, fundamentally altering the strategic calculus across the Middle East. No corroborating evidence, photographic documentation, or credible sourcing accompanies these assertions. Nevertheless, if even a fraction of the claim proves accurate, the ripple effects across global commodity markets, defense procurement budgets, and diplomatic alignments would be considerable. Observers are left to weigh the credibility of anonymous speculation against the magnitude of its implied geopolitical consequences.
clips.text_en_c2: /pol/ contends, with characteristic bombast and characteristic absence of corroboration, that China has commenced the overt transfer of what it terms 'superweapons' to Iran — armaments whose technological sophistication, the post insists, lies beyond the West's collective capacity for comprehension. The claim arrives freighted with geopolitical portent: the suggestion, unsubstantiated yet declamatory in delivery, is that vast quantities of such materiel are already en route and that the resulting recalibration of Middle Eastern power dynamics will prove both rapid and irreversible. No sources are cited, no photographic evidence proffered, no official statements referenced — merely the assertion, delivered as though self-evident, that the strategic landscape is undergoing fundamental transformation.

clips.text_zh: 4chan話creatine會甩頭髮、爆瘡、成塊面腫。好啦我今日啱啱買咗一罐lol。肥仔信話飲咗會肥，但佢自己都飲緊⋯⋯點算🙏
clips.text_en_b1: /fit/ argues creatine makes you bald, gives you face acne, and makes your gut and face look puffy and fat. The OP admits the only upside is lifting 5 to 10 percent more. So creatine is mostly side effects plus a small strength gain, he concludes.
clips.text_en_b2: /fit/ debates whether creatine actually delivers enough upside to justify its reputation, with the prevailing view holding that the compound causes hair loss, breakouts, and noticeable facial bloating. The poster concedes that the only genuine benefit is lifting roughly five to ten percent more weight during training sessions, which feels marginal compared to the laundry list of side effects involved. Meanwhile, another gymgoer swears the supplement makes you fat, despite clearly taking it himself, leaving the original poster caught between conflicting advice and freshly opened…
clips.text_en_c1: Persistent threads on /fit/ insist that creatine supplementation precipitates alopecia, exacerbates facial acne, and produces a characteristic bloated, puffy appearance that undermines any aesthetic gains earned through dedicated training. The original poster, having purchased a container earlier today, finds himself caught between anecdotal horror stories and the supplement's established ergogenic benefits. A fitness acquaintance who warned that creatine causes fat gain was himself consuming the compound throughout his cautionary lecture. The cognitive dissonance is considerable: if the purported side effects were genuinely severe, would informed practitioners continue incorporating the supplement into their regimens with such apparent enthusiasm?
clips.text_en_c2: /fit/ is presently engaged in a vigorous campaign against creatine monohydrate, enumerating its alleged offences with the prosecutorial zeal of a dietary inquisitor. Hair loss, facial acne, bloating, and a generalised impression of puffiness across both countenance and midsection — these constitute, according to the thread's consensus, the inevitable physiological toll exacted by supplementation. The OP, displaying admirable candour if not impeccable timing, confesses to having purchased a tin of the offending substance earlier that very day. The fat-acceptance advocate invoked as counterpoint — who insists creatine induces corpulence whilst apparently consuming it herself — provides, perhaps unwittingly, a rather elegant illustration of the contradictions endemic to online fitness discourse.
